body:
Why Mass and Weight Must Be Distinguished

In everyday conversation, mass and weight are often treated as the same quantity. In physics, they have different meanings, units and properties.

Mass

Mass is a measure of the inertia of a body. Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist a change in its state of rest or motion.

Mass also represents the quantity of matter in a body in the elementary school-level description.

The SI unit of mass is kilogram (kg). Mass is a scalar quantity, meaning it has magnitude but no direction.

The mass of an object remains unchanged when the object is taken from Earth to the Moon or another planet, provided no matter is added or removed.

A beam balance can compare an object's mass with known standard masses. Because both sides experience the same local gravitational acceleration, their comparison determines mass.

Weight

Weight is the gravitational force acting on an object due to Earth or another celestial body.

For an object of mass \(m\) at a location where the acceleration due to gravity is \(g\):

$$W=mg$$

Weight is a force. Therefore, its SI unit is newton (N), not kilogram.

Weight is a vector quantity because gravitational force has both magnitude and direction. Near Earth's surface, its direction is approximately vertically downward.

A spring balance can measure force and is commonly used to measure weight. Many everyday weighing scales display a mass value in kilograms by using an assumed relationship between weight and gravitational acceleration.

Mass and Weight Compared

FeatureMassWeight
MeaningMeasure of inertiaGravitational force
SymbolmW
SI unitKilogram (kg)Newton (N)
NatureScalarVector
Depends on locationNoYes
Typical instrumentBeam balanceSpring balance

Weight on Earth and the Moon

The Moon has a smaller mass and radius than Earth. Its surface gravitational acceleration is approximately 1.62 m s-2, compared with about 9.8 m s-2 on Earth.

Consequently, the weight of an object on the Moon is approximately 1/6 of its weight on Earth.

Consider an object whose mass is 10 kg.

Its weight on Earth is:

$$W_{\mathrm{Earth}}=10\times9.8=98\;\mathrm{N}$$

Its weight on the Moon is approximately:

$$W_{\mathrm{Moon}}=10\times1.62=16.2\;\mathrm{N}$$

The object's mass remains 10 kg in both places. Only its weight changes.

What Happens When an Object Is Taken to Another Place?

If the value of g increases, the weight of the same object increases. If g decreases, its weight decreases.

For example, an object's weight is slightly greater at Earth's poles than at the equator when other relevant conditions are comparable. Its mass is unchanged.

Similarly, the same object weighs less at a sufficiently high altitude than at Earth's surface because the gravitational acceleration becomes smaller.

Weightlessness or reduced weight does not imply that an object has lost its mass. Mass describes inertia, while weight describes gravitational force.

Useful Unit Relationship

Newton's second law states that force equals mass multiplied by acceleration. Therefore:

$$1\;\mathrm{N}=1\;\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$$

At a place where g = 9.8 m s-2, a mass of 1 kg has a weight of approximately 9.8 N.

Prelims focus

  • Mass is a measure of inertia and is measured in kilograms.
  • Weight is gravitational force and is measured in newtons.
  • Weight is calculated using \(W=mg\).
  • Mass remains unchanged when an object moves between Earth and the Moon.
  • Weight on the Moon is approximately 1/6 of weight on Earth.
  • Trap: A body with a mass of 10 kg does not have a weight of 10 N on Earth's surface.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 10, Gravitation, sections 10.3-10.4.1, printed pp. 137-138; GCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 9, Gravitation, sections 9.3-9.4.1, printed pp. 105-106; NASA Glenn Research Center, Moon, section on lunar surface gravitational acceleration, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The same object has identical mass but different weight on Earth and the Moon.

title: Mass and Weight: Meaning, Units and Their Relationship

body:
Why the Same Force Can Produce Different Effects

A person standing on loose sand may sink more deeply than the same person lying on the sand. A sharp knife cuts more easily than a blunt knife. A pointed nail enters wood more easily than its broad end.

These situations demonstrate that the effect of a force depends not only on its magnitude but also on the area over which it acts.

Meaning of Thrust

Thrust is the force acting perpendicular, or normal, to a surface.

Consider a book resting on a horizontal table. Its weight acts downward. The book exerts a downward force on the tabletop, perpendicular to the surface. This force is the thrust applied by the book to the table.

Thrust is a force, so its SI unit is the newton (N).

If the book is turned onto a different face while its mass remains unchanged, the magnitude of its weight and the thrust it applies to the horizontal table remain approximately the same. However, its area of contact may change.

Meaning of Pressure

Pressure is the perpendicular force acting per unit area of a surface.

Mathematically:

$$P=\frac{F}{A}$$

Here, \(P\) is pressure, \(F\) is thrust and \(A\) is the area over which the thrust acts.

The SI unit of pressure is pascal (Pa), named after Blaise Pascal.

$$1\;\mathrm{Pa}=1\;\mathrm{N/m^2}$$

How Pressure Changes With Force and Area

For a fixed contact area, pressure increases when the perpendicular force increases.

For a fixed perpendicular force, pressure increases when the contact area decreases.

  • If thrust doubles while area remains unchanged, pressure doubles.
  • If area doubles while thrust remains unchanged, pressure becomes half.
  • If area becomes 3 times larger while thrust remains unchanged, pressure becomes 1/3 of its original value.

Example: Same Force, Different Areas

Suppose a block applies a downward thrust of 60 N to a horizontal surface.

When the contact area is 0.02 m2:

$$P=\frac{60}{0.02}=3000\;\mathrm{Pa}$$

When the same block rests on a larger contact area of 0.06 m2:

$$P=\frac{60}{0.06}=1000\;\mathrm{Pa}$$

The force remains 60 N, but the pressure decreases from 3000 Pa to 1000 Pa because the contact area becomes 3 times larger.

Applications of Pressure in Daily Life

Sharp Knives and Pointed Nails

A sharp cutting edge has a small contact area. For the same applied force, this creates greater pressure and makes cutting or piercing easier.

Broad School-Bag Straps

A broad strap spreads the force of the bag over a larger area of the shoulder. This reduces pressure on the shoulder and makes the bag more comfortable to carry.

Wide Tyres and Tracks

Wide tyres and continuous tracks can distribute a vehicle's weight over a larger contact area. This reduces pressure on soft ground and helps prevent excessive sinking.

Camels Walking on Sand

A camel's broad feet spread its weight over a comparatively large contact area, reducing pressure on loose sand. This is one reason camels can move effectively on sandy ground.

Building Foundations

Wide foundations distribute the weight of a structure over a greater area of supporting soil. The resulting average pressure is smaller than it would be if the same load acted over a narrow area.

Thrust and Pressure Are Different Quantities

Thrust measures the total perpendicular force acting on a surface. Pressure measures how concentrated that force is over an area.

Consequently, 2 surfaces can experience the same thrust but different pressures. Conversely, 2 surfaces can experience the same pressure while the total thrust differs because their areas are different.

A smaller contact area does not increase the applied force by itself. It increases the pressure produced by the same perpendicular force.

Prelims focus

  • Thrust acts perpendicular to a surface.
  • Pressure equals thrust divided by contact area.
  • The SI unit of thrust is N.
  • The SI unit of pressure is Pa, equivalent to N/m2.
  • Sharp knives, broad straps, wide tyres and wide foundations illustrate the pressure-area relationship.
  • Trap: A decrease in contact area increases pressure when the applied thrust is kept unchanged.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 10, Gravitation, section 10.5, printed pp. 138-139; GCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 9, Gravitation, section 9.5, printed pp. 106-107; NCERT, Science, Class 8, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 11, Force and Pressure, section 11.8, printed pp. 137-138; GCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 8, Force and Pressure, section 8.8, printed pp. 103-104.]

pictures.alt: The same block applies 60 N: a 0.02 m² contact area produces 3000 Pa, while a 3 times larger area of 0.06 m² produces 1000 Pa.
pictures.caption: The same thrust produces greater pressure over a smaller area.

title: Thrust and Pressure: Why Area Changes the Effect of Force

body:
Why Liquids and Gases Exert Pressure

Liquids and gases are collectively called fluids because they can flow. Like solids, fluids can exert forces on surfaces. However, fluids can also exert pressure on the sides of their containers and on objects immersed in them.

Water stored in a tank presses against its bottom and walls. Air inside an inflated balloon pushes against the balloon's inner surface. These are familiar examples of fluid pressure.

Pressure in Liquids

A liquid at rest exerts pressure because of the forces acting within it, including the weight of the liquid above a given level.

At a particular depth in a stationary liquid, pressure acts in all directions. It acts perpendicular to the surface of any object or container wall in contact with that liquid.

Liquid Pressure Increases With Depth

Consider 2 points in the same tank of water. The deeper point has a greater height of water above it and therefore experiences greater liquid pressure.

Consequently, water emerging from a lower opening in a container can be driven out more strongly than water emerging from a higher opening, when other conditions are comparable.

Pressure at the Same Depth

In a stationary liquid of uniform density, points at the same depth experience the same pressure, provided they are under the same surrounding conditions.

This is true even when the container has an irregular shape. For a stationary liquid, pressure at a specified depth depends on the liquid and the depth, not simply on the total quantity of liquid or the shape of the container.

Effect of Liquid Density

At the same depth, a denser liquid generally produces greater pressure than a less dense liquid, when gravitational acceleration and surface pressure are the same.

Therefore, the pressure produced by a column of liquid depends on the liquid's density as well as its depth.

Pressure in Gases

Air and other gases exert pressure on the walls of their containers. Gas particles move continuously and interact with the surrounding surfaces, producing pressure.

When air is pumped into a bicycle tyre, the air exerts outward pressure against the tyre's inner surface. The tyre becomes firm because of this internal pressure.

Gases exert pressure in different directions, not only downward.

Pressure Transmission in a Confined Fluid

When additional pressure is applied to a fluid confined within a closed system, that pressure change is transmitted throughout the fluid. In the ideal elementary description, the transmitted pressure change is undiminished.

This principle is associated with Blaise Pascal and is commonly called Pascal's principle.

It is distinct from the basic observation that the pressure within a stationary liquid increases with depth. The first concerns transmission of an applied pressure change; the second concerns the liquid's pressure under gravity.

Atmospheric Pressure

Earth is surrounded by a layer of gases called the atmosphere. Atmospheric air has mass and is attracted by Earth. It therefore exerts pressure on objects and surfaces.

Atmospheric pressure is the pressure exerted by the air of Earth's atmosphere.

Near sea level, atmospheric pressure is approximately \(1.01\times10^5\;\mathrm{Pa}\), although actual pressure varies with altitude and weather conditions.

Atmospheric pressure generally decreases with increasing altitude because the amount of air above a given location becomes smaller.

Why the Atmosphere Does Not Crush Us

Atmospheric pressure acts on the human body from different directions. The fluids and gases within the body also exert pressure. Under normal conditions, these pressures are sufficiently balanced that the body is not crushed by the surrounding atmosphere.

How a Suction Cup Sticks to a Surface

When a flexible suction cup is pressed against a smooth surface, much of the air beneath it escapes. The pressure inside the cup becomes lower than the atmospheric pressure outside.

The greater external atmospheric pressure pushes the cup against the surface. The holding effect is caused by this pressure difference, rather than by the absence of all forces beneath the cup.

Why Air Moves

Differences in atmospheric pressure help drive the movement of air. Air generally moves from regions of higher pressure towards regions of lower pressure, with its actual motion also influenced by other atmospheric conditions.

This connects the elementary concept of pressure to the occurrence of winds without changing the physical meaning of pressure.

Prelims focus

  • Liquids and gases are fluids.
  • A stationary liquid exerts pressure on the bottom and sides of its container.
  • Liquid pressure increases with depth.
  • Pressure is equal at the same depth in the same stationary liquid under the same conditions.
  • Atmospheric pressure is exerted by the surrounding air.
  • Trap: Atmospheric pressure does not act only downward; air exerts pressure in all directions.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 11, Force and Pressure, sections 11.9-11.10, printed pp. 138-141; GCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 8, Force and Pressure, sections 8.9-8.10, printed pp. 104-107; NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 10, Gravitation, section 10.5.1, printed pp. 139-140; NCERT, Science, Class 7, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 8, Winds, Storms and Cyclones, sections 8.1-8.2, printed pp. 80-83.]
